summary: Describes the state of standardization of Internet protocols as determined by the Internet Architecture Board. It is a periodic status list. It is historic and was replaced by RFC 1780.

eli5.summary: A report card showing how official each internet rule had become.

subtitle: Status report on Internet protocol standardization as of November 1994

tldr.problem: The Internet community needs a current, authoritative source for understanding which protocols are standards, which are under development, and which are obsolete.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1720 catalogs all Internet protocols by standardization state (standard, draft standard, proposed standard, experimental, informational, historic) and requirement level (required, recommended, elective, limited use, not recommended), explains the process for advancing protocols, and lists the organizations and contacts responsible for standardization.
tldr.outcome: This periodic report served as the definitive reference for protocol standards status, though it became outdated quarterly and was periodically replaced with new versions like RFC 1780.

facts.label: Requirement levels
facts.value: 5 (Required, Recommended, Elective, Limited Use, Not Recommended)

today: RFC 1720 is Historic; it was replaced by RFC 1780 with updated protocol listings. The document served as the authoritative status report for Internet standardization at a snapshot in time. Modern references for current standards include the Online RFC Index and the IANA registry.

sections.title: What This Document Does
sections.content:
RFC 1720 is the Internet Official Protocol Standards document issued in November 1994. It describes the state of standardization of Internet protocols as determined by the Internet Architecture Board (IAB). The document was intended to be issued approximately quarterly, with an expiration date to prevent use of outdated copies.

The RFC begins with an explanation of the standardization process, the RFC document series, and reference documents like Assigned Numbers, Host Requirements, and Gateway Requirements. It then lists protocols organized by their current standardization state, with asterisks marking protocols that are new, moved, or changed since the previous edition.
sections.eli5: A guide that lists what protocols are official and why. It explains how the Internet decides which rules to use.

sections.title: The Standardization Process
sections.content:
The IAB maintains the list of standards documents and oversees the standardization process through the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) and Internet Research Task Force (IRTF), each with steering groups (IESG and IRSG). The process is detailed in RFC 1602.

Protocols progress through maturity levels: proposed standard, draft standard, and standard, each requiring increasing scrutiny. The IESG must recommend advancement at each step. Minimum delays of 6 months (proposed to draft) and 4 months (draft to standard) allow community review. Proposed standards require at least two independent implementations; promotion to standard generally requires operational experience and interoperability between multiple implementations.

Protocols that are no longer actively used or have been superseded are designated historic. Experimental protocols document early research work. Informational protocols describe work from other organizations or vendors published for community convenience. The terms standard, draft standard, and proposed standard are reserved for protocols the IESG has approved; vendor protocols, even if widely used, cannot use these terms without IESG recommendation.
sections.eli5: New protocols start as proposals. They move up through stages of testing, with waiting periods between. Once official, they can be promoted or moved aside if something better comes along.

sections.title: Protocol States and Statuses
sections.content:
Each protocol is assigned a state (maturity level) and a status (requirement level). The six states are: Standard (approved by IESG, assigned STD number), Draft Standard (under active consideration, substantial testing desired), Proposed Standard (may be considered for future standardization), Experimental (not to be implemented except by protocol developers), Informational (published for community convenience), and Historic (unlikely to become standards, superseded or unused).

The five requirement levels are: Required (must be implemented in all systems), Recommended (should be implemented), Elective (optional), Limited Use (inappropriate for some contexts), and Not Recommended (not advised for use). The specification notes that few protocols are required in all systems due to the wide variety of Internet devices (gateways, routers, terminal servers, workstations, hosts). The combination of state and status determines a protocol's role in the Internet standards track.
sections.eli5: Each protocol has a level (how official it is) and a requirement (whether you must, should, or don't need to use it). Different devices need different protocols.

sections.title: Protocol Lists and Recent Changes
sections.content:
The bulk of RFC 1720 consists of protocol listings organized by state. Section 6.2 lists Standard Protocols (subdividing between general protocols and network-specific standards). Section 6.3 covers Network-Specific Standard Protocols. Sections 6.4 and 6.5 list Draft Standard and Proposed Standard Protocols. Section 6.6 lists Telnet Options. Section 6.7 covers Experimental and Section 6.8 Informational Protocols. Section 6.9 lists Historic Protocols, and Section 6.10 covers obsolete protocols.

Section 6.1 details recent changes: new RFCs since the previous edition and other changes. For example, RFCs might be newly promoted, moved between categories, or revised. This section helps users understand what has changed since the last edition and identify which RFC to use for the current specification of each protocol.
sections.eli5: The document sorts all protocols into groups: official ones, ones being tested, ones for special uses, and old ones nobody uses anymore. It highlights what's new.

sections.title: Reference Documents and Contacts
sections.content:
RFC 1720 points to several important companion documents. The Assigned Numbers document (RFC 1700) lists assigned parameter values like IP protocol numbers and TCP port codes. Host Requirements documents (RFC 1122 for IPv4, RFC 1123 for applications) clarify and update protocol specifications. Gateway Requirements (RFC 1009) does the same for routers. These documents sometimes take precedence over earlier RFCs and the MIL-STD specifications.

The RFC also lists contact information for key organizations: the Internet Architecture Board, Internet Engineering Task Force, Internet Research Task Force, Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA), the RFC Editor, and the Network Information Center. It includes how to submit documents, obtain RFCs, and report protocol issues. This makes RFC 1720 both a catalog and a directory for the standardization process itself.
sections.eli5: The document tells you where to find more details, who to contact with questions, and how to submit new rules for consideration.
